{{smaller block|Wanton Cupid, idle ''toyer'',
Pleasing tyrant, soft destroyer.
{{right|''W. Harrison'', Passion of Sappho (Nichols's Collection), [IV. 183.}}}}

'''toyful''' (toi′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''toy'' + ''-ful.''] Full of idle sport; playful.

{{smaller block|It quickened next a ''toyful'' ape, and so
Gamesome it was, that it might freely go
From tent to tent, and with the children play.
{{right|''Donne'', Progress of the Soul, st. 46.}}}}

'''toyingly''' (toi′ing-li), ''adv.'' Triflingly; wantonly. ''Bailey'', 1731.

'''toyish''' (toi′ish), ''a.'' [< ''toy'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] 1†. Fit only for a plaything; trifling; fantastic; whimsical.

{{smaller block|''Capricciare'', to growe or be humorous, ''toish'', or fantastical.
{{right|''Florio'', 1598.}}}}

{{smaller block|Adieu, ye ''toyish'' reeds, that once could please
My softer lips, and lull my cares to ease.
{{right|''Pomfret'', Dies Novissima.}}}}

{{smaller block|The contention is trifling and ''toyish.''
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 320.}}}}

2. Toy-like; small: as, a ''toyish'' church.

'''toyishly''' (toi′ish-li), ''adv.'' In a toyish or trifling manner.

'''toyishness†''' (toi′ish-nes), ''n.'' Inclination to toy or trifle.

{{smaller block|Your society will discredit that ''toyishness'' of wanton fancy that plays tricks with words, and frolicks with the caprices of frothy imagination.
{{right|''Glanville'', Scep. Sci.}}}}

¶
'''toyl†''', '''toyle†''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' Old spellings of ''toil.''

'''toyman''' (toi′man), ''n.''; pl. ''toymen'' (-men). One who makes or sells toys.

{{smaller block|But what in oddness can be more sublime
Than Sloane, the foremost ''toyman'' of his time?
{{right|''Young'', Love of Fame, iv. 113.}}}}

'''toy-mutch''' (toi′much), ''n.'' A close linen or woolen cap, without lace, frill, or border, and with flaps covering the neck and part of the shoulders, worn chiefly by old women. Also ''toy.'' [Scotch.]

'''Toynbee's experiment.''' The exhaustion of air from the middle ear by swallowing when both the mouth and nostrils are closed.

'''toyo''' (toi′ō), ''n.'' [S. Amer.] A fragrant plant of British Guiana, an infusion and syrup of the leaves and stems of which are employed as a remedy in chronic coughs. ''Treas. of Bot.''

'''toyon''' (toi′on), ''n.'' The Californian holly, ''Heteromeles arbutifolia.'' Also ''tollon.''

'''toyous†''' (toi′us), ''a.'' [< ''toy'' + ''-ous.''] Trifling.

{{smaller block|Against the hare in all
Prove ''toyous.''
{{right|''Warner'', Albion's England, v. 27.}}}}

'''toy-shop''' (toi′shop), ''n.'' 1†. A shop where trinkets and fancy articles were sold.

{{smaller block|All the place about me was covered with packs of ribbon, brocades, embroidery, and ten thousand other materials, sufficient to have furnished a whole street of ''toyshops.'' {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 499.}}}}

{{smaller block|We stopped again at Wirman's, the well-known ''toyshop'' in St. James's Place. . . . He sent for me to come out of the coach, and help him to choose a pair of silver buckles.
{{right|''Boswell'', Johnson, an. 1778.}}}}

'''trabecular''' (trā-bek′ụ̄-lär), ''a.'' [< ''trabecule'' + ''-ar''<sup>3</sup>.] Of or pertaining to a trabecula; forming or formed by trabeculæ; trabeculate.

Has he never been courtier, my lord? ''Mo.'' Never, my lady. ''Be.'' And why did the ''toy'' take him in th' head now? {{right|''Chapman,'' Bussy D'Ambois, i. 1.}}}} 7. Same as ''toy-mutch.'' [Now Scotch.] {{smaller block|On my head no ''toy'' But was her pattern. {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Two Noble Kinsmen, i. 3.}}}} 8. In ''music,'' in old English writers, a dance-tune or other light, trifling piece.—9. A toy dog. {{smaller block|In the ''Toys'' equal first went to the well-known Wee Flower and a very good Black-and-tan called Little Jem. {{right|''The Field'' (London), Jan. 28, 1882. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}} {{smaller block|'''Philosophical toy,''' any device or contrivance, of no practical use, which serves to illustrate some fact or principle in natural science in an attractive or entertaining as well as instructive manner, as a contrivance for producing the effects of so-called natural magic. The bottle-imp is a good example. See cuts under ''Cartesian'' and ''phenakistoscope.''—'''Steel toys.''' See ''steel.''—'''To take toy†,''' to become restive; start.}} {{smaller block|The hot horse, hot as fire, ''Took toy'' at this, and fell to what disorder His power could give his will, bounds, comes on end. {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Two Noble Kinsmen, v. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|'''Toy dog,''' any dog bred to an unusually small or pygmy size and kept as a pet or plaything; a toy. Spaniels and terriers are so bred in some strains, and there are various mongrel toys.—'''Toy spaniel.''' See ''spaniel,'' 1.—'''Toy terrier,''' a terrier bred to small or pygmy size and kept as a plaything. Such terriers are usually of the black-and-tan variety, and some of them are among the smallest dogs known.}} {{smaller block|In-breeding is certain, if carried too far, to stunt the growth of any animal, and this is, without any doubt, the means by which the modern ''toy-terrier'' was first originated. {{right|''V. Shaw,'' Book of the Dog, xxii.}}}} '''toy''' (toi), ''v.'' [< ''toy'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To trifle; amuse one's self; play. {{smaller block|Some plaid with strawes; some ydly satt at ease;
But other some could not abide to ''toy''. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ix. 35.}} Pale dreamers, whose fantastic lay
''Toys'' with smooth trifles like a child at play. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Poetry.}}}} '''2.''' To dally amorously. {{smaller block|Aft on the banks we'd sit us thair,

''tracen'', < OF. ''tracer'', ''trasser'', delineate, score, trace, also follow, pursue, F. ''tracer'', trace, = Sp. ''trazar'' = Pg. ''traçar'', plan, sketch, = It. ''tracciare'', trace, devise, < ML. *''tractiare'', delineate, score, trace, freq. of L. ''trahere'', pp. ''tractus'', draw: see ''tract''1.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' 1. To draw; delineate; mark out, as on a map, chart, or plan; map out; design; sketch. {{smaller block|The Sea-works and Booms were ''traced'' out by Marquis Spinola.{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|We firmly believe that no British government has ever deviated from that line of internal policy which he [Lord Holland] has ''traced'', without detriment to the public.{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Holland.}}}} '''2.''' To write, especially by a careful or laborious formation of the letters; form in writing. {{smaller block|Every letter I ''trace'' tells me with what rapidity Life follows my pen.{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, ix. 8.}}}} {{smaller block|The signature of another plainly appeared to have been ''traced'' by a hand shaking with emotion.{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xiv.}}}} Specifically—'''3.''' To copy, as a drawing or engraving, by following the lines and marking them on a superimposed sheet, through which they appear. {{smaller block|There is an inscription round the inside of the [bronze] vase, which was ''traced'' of, as it is engraved on it, and shews exactly the circumference of the vase.{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 207.}}}} '''4.''' To cover with traced lines, as with writing or tracery. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The deep-set windows, stain'd and ''traced'', Would seem slow-flaming crimson fires From shadow'd grots of arches interlaced.{{right|''Tennyson'', Palace of Art.}}}} {{smaller block|And he holds a palm-leaf scroll in his hands, ''Traced'' with the Prophet's wise commands.{{right|''Whittier'', The Palm-Tree.}}}} '''5.''' To follow the track, trail, or path of; pursue: a general term, the verbs ''track'' and ''trail'' being more specific, as in hunting.
